title: The regulatory framework of the pest management industry

lessons.title: Why pest management is regulated
lessons.html:
A regulated profession

Pest management officers work with some of the most hazardous substances used in agriculture and in buildings: insecticides, rodenticides, herbicides and fumigant gases. Used correctly, these products protect grain stores, homes, food factories and farms. Used carelessly, they can kill people, poison water and wildlife, and leave illegal residues on food. For this reason pest management in South Africa is controlled by law, and every officer must understand the framework they work in.

The main purposes of regulation

  • Make sure only effective, evaluated products are sold and used.
  • Make sure products are applied only by people with the right training.
  • Protect workers, clients, the public and animals from poisoning.
  • Protect soil, water and biodiversity.
  • Keep food and export products within residue limits so that markets stay open.

Layers of the framework

The framework has several layers that work together:

  1. Acts of Parliament set out the broad rules and powers.
  2. Regulations under those Acts give the detailed requirements, such as registration of operators and labelling.
  3. The product label, approved at registration, is a legal document that states exactly how a product may be used.
  4. Standards and codes of practice, from industry bodies and standards organisations, describe good practice.
  5. Company procedures and client requirements, such as food safety audit schemes, add further rules.

Consequences of non-compliance

Breaking these rules can lead to criminal prosecution, fines, deregistration as an operator, civil claims for damages, loss of clients and contracts, and, most seriously, injury or death. A pest management officer who knows the law protects themselves, their employer and their clients.

lessons.title: Key legislation for pest management officers
lessons.html:
Act 36 of 1947

The Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947 is the core law for the industry. It is administered by the Registrar in the national Department of Agriculture. Under this Act:

  • Agricultural remedies, which include insecticides, fungicides, herbicides, rodenticides and fumigants, must be registered before they may be sold or used.
  • Each registered product carries a registration number on its label, and the label sets out the pests, crops or situations, rates and precautions for which it is registered.
  • Using a product in a way that is not according to the label is not allowed.
  • Persons who apply agricultural remedies for reward must be registered as pest control operators, in the category of work for which they are qualified, such as fumigation, wood destroying organisms, or structural and health pests.

Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993

The OHS Act requires employers to provide a safe workplace and employees to follow safety instructions and use PPE. The Regulations for Hazardous Chemical Agents made under the Act require risk assessments, exposure control, training, monitoring and record keeping where workers are exposed to hazardous chemicals.

Environmental laws

  • National Environmental Management Act 107 of 1998 (NEMA): a general duty of care to prevent pollution and environmental degradation.
  • National Environmental Management: Waste Act 59 of 2008: controls the storage, transport and disposal of waste, including hazardous chemical waste and empty containers.
  • National Water Act 36 of 1998: protects water resources from pollution.
  • National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004: includes the regulations on alien and invasive species that shape weed and invader plant work.

Other relevant laws

The Hazardous Substances Act 15 of 1973 controls certain hazardous substances. The Agricultural Pests Act 36 of 1983 deals with the control of plant pests, including import controls. Officers working for clients also need to be aware of the Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008.

lessons.title: Compliance in day-to-day practice
lessons.html:
Turning law into practice

Knowing the names of Acts is not enough. Compliance happens in the daily decisions an officer makes.

Registration and competence

  • Keep your own pest control operator registration current and work only within your registered category.
  • Unregistered staff may assist only under the conditions set out in the regulations and your company procedures; check what supervision is required.
  • Keep records of your training and refresher courses.

The label is the law

Before every job, confirm the product is registered for the specific pest and situation, and apply it at the label rate and by the label method. Observe all label precautions, re-entry intervals and, where food or crops are involved, withholding periods. If the label does not cover the situation, do not use the product.

Records

Typical records required by law, by clients or by audit schemes include:

RecordTypical content
Treatment recordDate, site, pest, product, registration number, quantity, method, operator
Chemical stock registerReceipts, issues and balance of each product
Risk assessmentsHazards, controls and PPE for each type of job
Training recordsCourses, dates and registration details
Incident reportsSpills, exposures, complaints and corrective action

Working with clients and inspectors

Clients such as food factories, silos and exporters are audited. They will ask for your registration, product labels and SDSs, and treatment records. Inspectors from the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Employment and Labour may also visit. Keep documents organised and cooperate openly.

Staying current

Regulations, product registrations and approved uses change. Products can be withdrawn. Keep in touch with your industry association, suppliers and the Registrar's notices.

Key points

  • Act 36 of 1947 requires registration of agricultural remedies and of operators who apply them for reward.
  • The registered label is a legal document; use products only as the label allows.
  • The OHS Act 85 of 1993 and its hazardous chemical regulations protect workers.
  • Environmental laws, including NEMA, the Waste Act and the National Water Act, prohibit pollution.
  • Keep complete treatment, stock, training and incident records.
